tldr: We propose a world action model that simultaneously predicts hand contact forces and torques (wrenches) alongside motion and vision, directly using the predicted forces as reference values for admittance control to dramatically stabilize millimeter-level insertions and force-sensitive tasks.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of CW-WAM. In addition to images, language, and robot state, it takes past motion and contact wrench histories as input to jointly predict future video, motion, and wrenches using a Diffusion Transformer. The predicted motion and wrenches are sent to downstream high-speed force feedback control.
overview:
World Action Models (WAMs), which predict surrounding video and the next actions together, are drawing significant attention. However, relying solely on camera images makes it impossible to distinguish whether a peg is stuck on the rim of a hole or fully inserted to the bottom. It is also difficult to lift objects that look identical but have drastically different weights. For tasks where force modulation is key, force and torque (wrench) information from wrist force sensors is essential.

To address this, the authors developed CW-WAM, which jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench within a single model. Inspired by classical hybrid motion–force control, it pairs past motion commands with measured wrenches over time to predict time-aligned future motion chunks (sequences of targets) and wrench chunks. Furthermore, they built a slow–fast execution framework that directly uses the predicted wrench trajectory as reference values for an outer-loop 20-Hz admittance controller (which softly compliant-shifts the target position according to external forces).

In experiments on a real Franka arm, in a square peg insertion task with only 1-mm clearance per side, CW-WAM dramatically improved the success rate to 70%, compared to 25% for a conventional WAM without wrench input. In power adapter insertion into a wall socket, the success rate rose from 40% to 95%. Moreover, combining it with an admittance controller suppressed force fluctuations, demonstrating that smooth and natural contact motions can be realized.
contributions: Proposed CW-WAM, a structured contact-wrench world action model that synchronously predicts video, motion trajectories, and contact wrenches within the same Diffusion Transformer.

Introduced a pair-causal attention mechanism that preserves the causal relationship between motion and wrench, as well as a long fixed-length wrench memory that retains past contact history over 10 seconds.

Established a slow–fast control system that uses predicted wrench trajectories directly as references to perform online corrections via an admittance controller without training an extra residual correction policy.
Achieved high success rates and high-precision contact force control across four real-robot tasks: 1-mm clearance peg insertion, power adapter insertion, whiteboard wiping, and load-adaptive lifting.

sections.heading: Why Do Robot World Models Need "Force"?
sections.summary: While world action models predicting video and motion simultaneously are promising, vision alone cannot capture contacts or weight differences. Therefore, inspired by hybrid motion–force control, CW-WAM structures and jointly predicts motion and contact wrench. The predicted wrench acts as a reference for high-speed admittance control, maintaining smooth and safe force control even between model queries.
sections.details:
A World Action Model (WAM), where a robot plans actions while predicting environmental changes, is a powerful framework for intuitive and coherent motion planning. However, vision-only models have a critical weakness. For instance, when inserting a square peg into a hole, it may look "properly and fully inserted" due to camera blind spots or shadows even if it is stuck midway on the rim. In addition, when identical-looking boxes differ in weight by over tenfold, vision alone cannot determine the necessary lifting force.

For tasks involving contact and force modulation, force and torque information (wrench) obtained from a wrist force-torque sensor is indispensable. Prior studies have attempted to use wrench as an input, but this work takes it a step further: instead of just predicting how to move next, the model also predicts what forces will be exerted back on the end-effector when taking that action.

CW-WAM takes inspiration from classical hybrid motion–force control (a control method that separates position-controlled and force-controlled directions) to treat motion and wrench as structured pairs. It combines this with a slow–fast execution system where a 20-Hz admittance controller and a 1-kHz joint impedance controller fill the gaps between low-speed model inferences (approx. 2 Hz). This allows the system to instantly yield to unexpected overloads on the end-effector even while the model is running heavy computations, sustaining safe and high-precision contact manipulation.

sections.heading: From Visuomotor Policies to Force Prediction and Hybrid Control
sections.summary: This section organizes three related lineages: vision-based world model research, policy learning incorporating force or touch, and slow–fast control combining planners with high-speed feedback. CW-WAM stands out by jointly predicting motion and wrench and directly feeding the predictions as references into a classical, training-free admittance controller.
sections.details:
### Visuomotor Policies and World Action Models (WAMs)
Methods generating robot joint commands directly from camera images and language instructions have made remarkable progress. More recently, world action models (such as DreamZero) that generate actions while simulating future videos in their "minds" have emerged. However, existing WAMs basically model only vision and motion, unable to handle physical contact forces directly.

### Contact-Aware Policies and Motion–Wrench Prediction
Numerous studies feed force or tactile sensing into robots as input (e.g., ForceVLA, ManipForce). More advanced works (e.g., FAWAM, Facet-0) predict wrenches alongside motion. However, existing methods train a separate residual correction network to leverage the predicted wrench, or use it as a critic for action evaluation. In contrast, CW-WAM feeds the predicted wrench directly as a reference into a classical admittance controller. The key difference is achieving control-theoretically stable contact manipulation without needing to train an extra correction network.

### Slow–Fast Execution and Contact Feedback
When a robot performs contact-rich tasks, the contact state changes drastically within milliseconds. Yet, running large neural networks at hundreds of Hz is computationally impossible. Thus, slow–fast architectures combining a slow high-level planner with fast local feedback have been viewed as effective. CW-WAM adopts this concept, seamlessly unifying large model inference at roughly 0.5-second intervals, 20-Hz admittance corrections, and 1-kHz joint impedance control.

sections.heading: How Are Motion and Force Predicted Simultaneously?
sections.summary: Built upon a Diffusion Transformer, CW-WAM takes past motion and wrench pairs as inputs to jointly predict future video, motion, and wrenches. Key designs include pair-causal attention that preserves the physical causality where motion precedes force, and a long-term wrench memory that retains 10 seconds of past contact history. It is trained via flow matching and optimized with a loss normalized by the effective number of channels.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation and Shared Backbone
At observation time $t$, CW-WAM receives RGB images $V_t$, robot state $s_t$ (end-effector pose and gripper width), language instruction $\ell$, recent motion–wrench history $\mathcal{H}_t^{AW}$, and long-term wrench memory $\mathcal{H}_t^W$. It simultaneously predicts future video latents $\hat{Z}_t^+$, motion chunk $\hat{A}_t = (\hat{a}_{t,i})_{i=1}^H$, and contact wrench chunk $\hat{W}_t = (\hat{w}_{t,i})_{i=1}^H$ for the next $H$ steps. Here, each motion action $a_{t,i} \in \mathbb{R}^{10}$ comprises position, 6D continuous rotation representation, and gripper position, while each wrench $\hat{w}_{t,i} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ represents bias- and gravity-compensated 3-axis force and 3-axis torque in the end-effector frame. The backbone adopts the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B DiT (Diffusion Transformer) with approximately 5 billion parameters.

### III-B Interaction Module and Paired Prediction
To properly capture contact states, the input history is carefully handled. In the recent history (1.6 seconds, 24 segments at 15 Hz), high-rate (150 Hz) wrench measurements (up to 16 samples) are temporally paired with each motion command token and encoded. In addition, a Long-Term Wrench Memory (LTM) spanning the past 10 seconds is introduced to preserve memory of sustained tension or resistance forces when pulling objects.
The highlight of the future prediction part is Pair-Causal Attention (PC). In the self-attention mechanism, a lower-triangular mask is applied to the future sequence $[A_1^+, W_1^+, A_2^+, W_2^+, \ldots]$. In other words, the attention structure directly bakes in the causality where "force $W_i^+$ can attend to its paired motion $A_i^+$ and earlier history, but motion $A_i^+$ cannot directly attend to the concurrently predicted force $W_i^+$". This design reflects the physical law of causality: reaction forces return from the environment because the robot moves, not the other way around.

### III-C Training and Inference
The model is trained using Flow Matching. Independent noise is added to each modality (video, motion, wrench) to predict velocity fields. A critical detail here is loss normalization. By introducing effective-channel normalization, which divides the loss by the effective dimensionality of motion (10 channels) and wrench (6 channels), gradient imbalances across modalities are prevented. During real-robot inference, denoising is performed with 4 Euler steps, generating a 1.6-second future motion–wrench chunk in just 0.5 to 0.6 seconds.

captions.F2: Detailed architecture of CW-WAM. In addition to multimodal inputs (images, language, robot state), past motion–wrench history and long-term wrench memory (LTM) are provided. The pair-causal attention mask inside the DiT enables joint generation while preserving the physical causality between future motion and wrench.

sections.heading: Putting Predicted Forces into Action: The Slow–Fast System
sections.summary: To translate predicted motion and wrench pairs into robot control, a multi-stage architecture with a 20-Hz admittance controller and a 1-kHz joint impedance controller is formed. Using the predicted wrench as a reference, the end-effector nominal pose is adjusted online based on the error with measured wrenches, achieving smooth tracking without jamming.
sections.details:
### IV-A Admittance Control with Predicted Wrench
For the nominal end-effector pose $(p^{\mathrm{nom}}, R^{\mathrm{nom}})$ output by the model, admittance correction is performed using the wrench deviation $e_w$ between the predicted wrench $\hat{w}$ and measured wrench $w^{\mathrm{meas}}$. In the end-effector frame, the admittance controller is modeled as a system with virtual mass $M$, damping $C$, and stiffness $K_a$ as follows:
$M \Delta \ddot{x} + C \Delta \dot{x} + K_a \Delta x = S e_w + k_I \eta$
Here, $S$ is a diagonal selection matrix according to task-specific contact constraints, and $\eta$ is an error integral term. For example, in the peg insertion task, the weight along the insertion direction ($Z$-axis) is kept small to avoid hindering forward motion, while weights in lateral and rotational directions are set larger to quickly resolve hole misalignment and tilting. The calculated pose correction $\Delta x$ is added to the nominal pose and converted into target joint positions via inverse kinematics (IK).

### IV-B Continuous Chunk Execution and Trajectory Interpolation
A single model inference takes about 0.5 to 0.6 seconds, but the robot cannot simply stop moving. Thus, until a new prediction chunk arrives, the robot holds the terminal pose of the previous chunk while keeping admittance control active. Once a new chunk arrives, a $C^2$-continuous (continuous up to acceleration) connecting trajectory is generated to smoothly transition from the currently executing pose, velocity, and acceleration. Furthermore, progress alignment is introduced to advance the index of the reference wrench according to the progress of the end-effector position, ensuring appropriate force references are selected even with motion delays. The final joint trajectory is replanned every 50 ms via quintic splines and tracked with high precision by a 1-kHz joint impedance controller.

captions.F3: Slow–fast motion–force control pipeline. Receiving motion–wrench pairs from CW-WAM, the 20-Hz admittance controller corrects the end-effector pose online. Subsequently, commands are sent to the 1-kHz joint impedance controller via quintic polynomial interpolation while preserving $C^2$ continuity.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Validation: How Much Did Force Prediction Boost Success?
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across four real-robot tasks (peg insertion, adapter insertion, whiteboard wiping, and load-adaptive lifting). Compared with conventional WAM, CW-WAM dramatically increased success rates from 25% to 70% in peg insertion, and from 40% to 95% in adapter insertion. Combining admittance control substantially reduced force errors and fluctuations, also demonstrating accurate adaptation to weight differences in identical-looking boxes.
sections.details:
### V-A Task Setup and Data Collection
A Franka Research 3 arm was used to conduct four tasks:
- **Square Peg Insertion**: Only 1-mm clearance per side (a 38-mm peg into a 40-mm hole, depth ~50 mm). Slight tilts immediately cause jamming.
- **Power Adapter Insertion**: Grasping an adapter from a table and inserting it into a wall socket.
- **Whiteboard Wiping**: Erasing marker strokes with an eraser, requiring proper normal force against the surface.
- **Lifting a Box with a Spring Scale**: Lifting identical-looking boxes of different weights (30 g and 830 g) over a basket rim. The heavier box stretches the spring and must be lifted higher.
A total of 450 episodes were collected via bilateral teleoperation for training data.

### V-B & V-C Open-Loop Prediction Accuracy and Ablations
In prediction accuracy tests on test data (Table II), CW-WAM without LTM significantly reduced contact position error from 25.50 mm to 19.92 mm and force RMSE from 3.03 N to 2.84 N compared to a baseline that simply concatenates motion and wrench (WAM + Wrench). Removing pair-causal attention (PC) degraded position error by 2.96 mm, confirming the benefit of explicitly incorporating causal structure. Full CW-WAM with long-term memory (LTM) achieved the best force vector RMSE of 2.79 N.

### V-D & V-E Real-Robot Task Performance and Contact Behavior
Real-robot results were remarkably clear. While the baseline WAM without wrench input managed only a 25% (5/20) success rate on peg insertion, CW-WAM surged to 70% (14/20). In power adapter insertion, CW-WAM achieved 95% (19/20) versus 40% (8/20) for WAM. Successful position tracking RMSE on peg insertion improved substantially from 12.5 mm to 2.8 mm. Force profiles (Figure F5) reveal that while the baseline produced violent force spikes (collisions) during search, CW-WAM smoothly located the hole with appropriate force modulation.

### V-F Load-Adaptive Lifting
In the spring scale task (Figure F6), CW-WAM adapted lifting height remarkably across the two visually indistinguishable loads. For the light load (30 g), the median lift height was 423.6 mm (demonstration median: 420.9 mm), and for the heavy load (830 g), it was 481.8 mm (demonstration: 492.7 mm), accurately replicating the height needed to clear the rim. In contrast, vision-only WAM lifted to the same height regardless of weight, colliding with the rim on the heavy box and failing.

### V-G Effects of Admittance Control with Predicted Wrench
Pairing full CW-WAM with admittance control further improved force tracking accuracy. Force-reference RMSE dropped from 4.8 N to 2.7 N in peg insertion, and from 2.0 N to 1.3 N in wiping. Contact force standard deviation also halved from 1.86 N to 0.94 N in peg insertion, proving that tasks can be executed while maintaining stable contact without chattering.

captions.F5: Contact force profiles across tasks. The solid line (green) is CW-WAM with admittance control, maintaining smooth forces close to the demonstration reference (black line and gray band). In contrast, baseline methods (dashed lines) show excessive forces and sharp spikes.
captions.F6: Results for the spring-scale lifting task. Even with identical visual appearances, CW-WAM (blue) senses weight through wrist force feedback, lifting higher for the heavy box (left) and lower for the light box (right) to properly clear the basket rim (dashed line).

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Toward Genuine Physical AI
sections.summary: By combining structured joint prediction of motion and contact wrench with slow–fast control, CW-WAM has significantly advanced force-sensitive manipulation. Currently, admittance gains are tuned manually and evaluations remain in-distribution; learning the control parameters themselves and generalizing to unseen objects and tasks remain future challenges.
sections.details:
This paper introduced CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Equipped with pair-causal attention and long-term wrench memory in its interaction module, it enables high-precision contact manipulation and load-adaptive behavior, achieving success rates that overwhelmingly surpass conventional approaches in real-robot experiments. Furthermore, using predicted wrench trajectories as references in an admittance controller demonstrated stable force control while absorbing model inference latency.

On the other hand, the authors candidly point out several limitations and future topics. First, admittance control gains (virtual stiffness and damping) and the selection matrix $S$ for compliant directions are currently tuned manually per task. Moving forward, the model should predict these control gains and contact frames alongside motion and wrench to achieve true end-to-end closed-loop control. In addition, all experiments were conducted within the demonstration data distribution, leaving zero-shot generalization to novel object geometries and new environments as an important direction for future research.

takeaways: Incorporating force and torque prediction into World Action Models (WAMs) enables contact tasks impossible with vision alone, such as millimeter-level insertions and weight adaptation.
Baking the physical causality that "motion precedes force" into the model structure via an attention mask (Pair-Causal Attention) is remarkably effective.
Directly feeding predicted force trajectories as targets for admittance control realizes safe, smooth contact feedback without training additional residual correction networks.

The slow–fast architecture, pairing slow foundation model inference (~2 Hz) with fast controllers (20 Hz / 1 kHz), can serve as a powerful standard design pattern for deploying heavy world models on real robots.
limitations: Admittance control gains (virtual stiffness and damping) and directional selection matrices are tuned manually for each task.

Evaluations are limited to in-distribution settings close to training demonstrations (identical objects and environments); zero-shot generalization to unseen objects or different contact dynamics is not verified.

Because model inference requires 0.5 to 0.6 seconds even on a high-end GPU (RTX 5090), instantaneous reflexive behavior against sudden, abrupt collisions relies on the passive compliance of low-level force controllers.
